Notes: Earliest (probable) attestation: Obadiah 20 "Exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad (SPRD) shall possess the cities of the Negeb"; Wilken states Jews first settled in Sardis as early as the 6th or 5th c. BCE on this basis, Sepharad being the Aramaic name for Sardis per a bilingual Aramaic-Lydian inscription found in 1916 (KAI 260). Year = c. midpoint of 6th-5th c. BCE. Year Established -500 rests on this identification (probable, not certain). Presence of exiles only; no indication of size.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Sardis): Sardis (Sfard in Lydian and Persian) is most probably the Sepharad of Obadiah 20, so the community may go back to the Persian period (547-334 BCE). After Antiochus III destroyed and rebuilt the city (215-213 BCE) his viceroy Zeuxis brought in Jewish settlers from Mesopotamia. Year c. 213 BCE (end of the rebuilding; settlement shortly after). Settlement of Jewish colonists; no count for Sardis.

Josephus, Antiquities 12.147-149: letter of Antiochus III to Zeuxis (who governed from Sardis) ordering 2000 Jewish families with their effects moved from Mesopotamia and Babylon to the fortresses of Lydia and Phrygia because of a revolt there. 2000 families (~10000 persons) is a REGIONAL figure for Lydia and Phrygia; Sardis is not named, so Population left blank. Date c. 210 BCE (Antiochus III in the upper satrapies, c. 212-205 BCE). Authenticity debated (Schalit defends it).

Encyclopaedia Judaica: a decree cited by Josephus shows the Jewish community at Sardis had a place of assembly, and another decree makes it certain there was a synagogue not later than the 1st c. BCE (year = midpoint of 1st c. BCE). The same article calls the community large and wealthy, 'probably several thousand in a city of c. 100,000', but bases this on the huge synagogue discovered in 1962, which belongs to the late Roman period (renovated c. 400 CE, destroyed 616 CE); this qualitative estimate is not a dated Second Temple-period figure, so Population left blank.

Jewish Encyclopedia (Sardis): community origins unknown but influential by the second half of the 1st c. BCE. Decree of the proquaestor and propraetor Lucius Antonius (Josephus, Ant. 14.10.17 = 14.235), dated 50-49 BCE: the Jews (Roman citizens) had 'an assembly of their own, according to the laws of their forefathers' and a place of their own where they settled disputes; privileges confirmed. Organized community with its own meeting place; no count.

Eilers on Josephus, Ant. 14.231-232: after the ruling exempting Jewish Roman citizens from military service under the consul L. Cornelius Lentulus (dated 49 BCE), 'The Sardians also passed a similar decree concerning us.' Eilers notes that Sardis 'did, after all, have a large and important Jewish population' (citing Mitchell 1993; Seager and Kraabel 1983). Presence of Jewish Roman citizens; no count.

Jewish Encyclopedia (Caesar, chronology of documents): Decree of the Sardians (Josephus, Ant. 14.259-261), dated 46-45 BCE (year c. -46): on the praetors' representation the Jews who are fellow citizens and live in the city were granted religious liberty, a place set apart for public worship 'with their wives and children', and the market officials were directed to admit food fit for them. Organized community with families and a designated place of worship; no count.

Letter of the proconsul Gaius Norbanus Flaccus to the magistrates of Sardis (Josephus, Ant. 16.171), dated by this source to c. 35 BCE (the Jewish Encyclopedia instead places it early in Augustus' reign): Caesar ordered that the Jews not be prevented from assembling and from sending monies to Jerusalem according to their ancestral custom. Community contributing to the Jerusalem Temple; no count.
